title: Breaking things on purpose
teaches: Timeouts, retries with backoff and jitter, retry storms, circuit breakers, bulkheads, load shedding, and Chaos Monkey

blocks.text: In August 2008 Netflix still made most of its money mailing DVDs, and a corruption in one of its main databases stopped it shipping them for three days. The company drew a lesson that shaped the next eight years: a single big database in its own datacentre was a single point of failure, and the way out was to move to Amazon Web Services and build every service on the assumption that any machine it ran on could disappear at any moment. The move took until January 2016.[^migration]

Assuming failure is easy to write in a design document and hard to make true, because the code that handles failure is the code that never runs. So in 2010 Netflix's engineers wrote a program that made it run. **Chaos Monkey** picked virtual machines in the production fleet at random and switched them off, during working hours, when the engineers who owned them were at their desks. It ran in production because a test environment has the code but not the traffic, the data or the real behaviour of the services each one calls. A service that could not lose a machine without users noticing would be found out on a Tuesday afternoon instead of at three in the morning.

On 21 April 2011 Amazon's largest region, in northern Virginia, had a long outage of its block storage service. Sites that ran there went down for hours, some for days. Netflix ran there too, and kept streaming with higher error rates and no large outage, which its engineers put down in part to having practised losing machines.[^aws] That is the practice to take from Netflix: **test failure on purpose**. This lesson's subject is the failure Chaos Monkey's first version did not test, and the one that takes down large systems most often: not a machine that dies, but one that gets slow.

A service that serves users usually calls several others. Take an API server at 1,000 requests a second. Half are "start playback" and call a catalogue service, 20 ms. The other half are "home page" and call the catalogue (20 ms) and then a recommendations service (normally 30 ms), 50 ms in all. In the figure below the catalogue is service A and recommendations is service B. Each request holds one of the server's 200 threads for as long as it takes.

By lesson 2's Little's law, threads in use = arrival rate × time each is held. Normally that is 500 × 0.02 + 500 × 0.05 = 35 threads of 200. Now the recommendations service slows to 3 seconds: a bad deploy, a full disk, a garbage collector, a dependency of its own. The home pages now hold a thread for 3.02 s each: 500 × 3.02 = 1,510 threads wanted, of 200. The pool fills in under half a second. From then on every request waits for a thread, including the playback requests that never touch recommendations. A service that was merely slow has taken down one that was perfectly healthy.

The cause is one missing number. Many client libraries ship with no timeout at all, or one of a minute, so a call to a slow service waits as long as the service does.[^default] A **timeout** bounds how long any call may hold a thread. Set it from the dependency's measured latency (lesson 9's percentiles): a little above its 99.9th percentile, so that healthy calls almost never hit it. A 99.9th percentile is the slowest call in a thousand, so it needs many thousands of samples to be steady: at 500 calls a second, a few minutes of measurements. If B's 99.9th percentile is 250 ms, a timeout of 300 ms fits. And decide what a timed-out call returns. A home page without personal recommendations can show a list of popular titles: a **fallback**, honest about being degraded, is better than an error.

blocks.caption: An API server's thread pool and two services it calls, one of which slows down. The model works out threads in use by Little's law; numbers are illustrative.
blocks.task: Slow B to a second or more, then add guards until every playback request is answered

blocks.text: With B at 3 seconds and no guards, playback falls to about 13%: the pool's 200 threads go to whoever got one first, and seven in eight requests time out at the user. Turn on the timeout alone and playback recovers fully, the home pages go out without recommendations, and the pool runs at 170 of 200. That margin is thinner than it looks, as the next guard shows.

A **retry** recovers from a fault that will not happen twice: a dropped packet, a machine that died mid-call, a leader election. It does nothing for a fault that will happen every time, such as a service that is slow because it is overloaded, and then it does harm. Turn on "Retry ×3" with the timeout in the figure. It means three tries in all, the first and two retries, each cut off at 300 ms, with waits of 50 ms and then 100 ms between them: each home page now holds its thread for 20 + 3 × 300 + 150 ms, about 1.07 s. The pool fills again, playback drops to about a third, and the slow service gets more calls than before. Retrying made the outage worse.
In a chain of services it is worse still. A request at the top passes through several layers, and if each layer retries its own calls, the retries multiply.

blocks.caption: How many calls one request can become, at the bottom of a chain where every call fails.

blocks.text: Three tries at each of five layers is 3⁵ = 243 calls at the bottom for every one at the top, and they arrive exactly when the bottom service is already failing. This is a **retry storm**, and it is why a service that briefly hiccups can stay down after the hiccup is over: the load from retries alone keeps it overloaded. The cures are rules about where retries happen. Retry at one layer only, usually the one nearest the user. Cap the number of tries. Give each client a **retry budget**: it counts its calls and its retries over a recent window, say ten seconds, and allows a retry only while retries are under a tenth of calls, so that when most calls are failing the client stops adding retries instead of tripling its load.[^budget] Retry only calls that are safe to repeat, which lesson 22 takes up.

The time between retries matters as much as their number. A client that retries at once, again and again, keeps hitting a server that needs a moment. **Exponential backoff** doubles the wait after each failure, 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, up to a cap. But if a hundred clients failed at the same moment, they back off by the same amounts and return at the same moments, a synchronised wave each time, and an overloaded server answers fewer of a wave the larger it is.

In March 2015 Marc Brooker of Amazon Web Services wrote up the fix on the AWS Architecture Blog: add **jitter**, randomness in the wait. With "full jitter" each client waits a random time between zero and its current backoff, so the hundred spread out across the interval instead of arriving together. His simulations showed it cutting both the total calls and the time until every client got through.

blocks.caption: A hundred clients fail at the same moment and retry. The server takes 20 calls a tenth of a second; sent n more than that, it serves only 20 × 20 / n, so 100 at once get 4 through. A client that fails waits 100 ms, or with backoff 100 ms doubled at each failure up to 3.2 s. Illustrative numbers.
blocks.task: Compare the three, ending with jitter

blocks.text: Retrying at once gets everyone through in about three seconds at the cost of nearly a thousand calls. Plain backoff sends fewer calls, but the waves stay synchronised and some clients are still failing eight seconds later. Backoff with jitter finishes in just over a second with fewer calls than either. The same synchronisation shows up anywhere many machines act on the same clock: caches expiring together (lesson 15), cron jobs at midnight, phones reconnecting after a network blip. The fix is always to spread the moments with a little randomness.

In 2007 Michael Nygard's book *Release It!* gave names to two guards that came from older engineering. A **circuit breaker** wraps calls to one dependency and counts failures. While calls succeed it is closed and passes them through. When failures pass a threshold, say half of calls over a few seconds with at least some minimum number of calls so that two failures out of three do not count, it opens: every call fails at once, without waiting, and goes to the fallback. After a pause, say five seconds, it is half-open: it lets a few calls through to test the dependency, closes if they succeed, and opens again if they fail. The figure's breaker opens after a second of failures and stays open five seconds. Failing fast frees the caller's threads immediately, and it takes the load off the struggling service, which gives it room to recover.[^fuse]

A **bulkhead** is named after the walls that divide a ship's hull into compartments, so one breach floods one compartment. In software it is a separate, limited pool for calls to each dependency, here 40 threads for B. Size it from normal use by Little's law: 500 calls a second × 30 ms is 15 threads, so 40 lets B get nearly three times slower before any call to it is refused. When B is slow, its 40 fill and further calls to B are refused at once; the other 160 threads keep serving everything else. Netflix packaged timeouts, breakers, bulkheads and fallbacks in a library called Hystrix and open-sourced it in 2012; every call from its API servers to another service went through one.

In the figure, the breaker alone or the bulkhead alone protects playback. They are not the same thing. The breaker reacts after a second of failures and then skips B entirely, recommendations included, until a test succeeds. The bulkhead never skips B, so the fastest of B's answers still get through, but it keeps 40 threads tied up waiting on it. Real systems use timeouts, a bulkhead and a breaker together.

The last guard protects a service from its own callers. When a server is overloaded, the work it does on a request that will time out anyway is wasted, and the queue it builds makes every request late (lesson 2). **Load shedding** refuses work early and cheaply: answer "busy, try later" in microseconds, before reading the request body or touching a database, once the queue or the CPU passes a limit. Done by priority, it drops the work that matters least first: prefetching and analytics before a user waiting for a video to start. A wrong design that looks similar is a health check that takes a slow server out of the load balancer: its load moves to the others, which slow down in turn and are taken out too, until nothing is left.[^sps]

Every guard in this lesson is code that runs only when something is wrong, which is why it so often fails when it is finally needed: a timeout set to the wrong value, a fallback that throws, a breaker that never opens. Chaos Monkey's point was to make that code run all the time. In July 2011 Netflix described a family of such tools, the Simian Army. Latency Monkey added delays to calls between services, the slow-dependency case this lesson started from. Chaos Gorilla took out a whole availability zone, one of a region's separate datacentres. Chaos Monkey itself was released as open source in July 2012.

Netflix later wrote down the method as **chaos engineering**. Pick a number that says the system is healthy, one users would agree with; Netflix used stream starts per second. State a hypothesis: if this fails, that number will not move. Inject the failure in production, on a small share of traffic first, and watch the number. If it moves, you have found a weakness on your own schedule, with people ready, and with a way to stop the experiment at once. Lesson 23 takes up how to keep any one failure, deliberate or not, from reaching every user.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on failing gracefully
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: An API server takes 500 requests a second, each calling a service that normally answers in 20 ms. The service slows to 2 s and the API has no timeout. What happens to the API's threads?
choices: They rise from about 10 to about 1,000, so a pool of a few hundred fills and even requests that skip that service wait
They stay at about 10, because each thread waits for the slow call without doing any work of its own
They double, from about 10 to about 20, because each request now takes longer while arriving at the same rate as before
items.why: Little's law: threads = rate × time held. 500 × 0.02 = 10; 500 × 2 = 1,000. Once the pool is full, requests queue for threads regardless of what they call.

items.ask: Five layers of services each retry failed calls up to three times. Why can this keep a struggling service at the bottom down?
choices: Retries are sent at a higher priority than first tries, so they push the service's ordinary work to the back of its queue
Each layer's retries multiply the one below, up to 3⁵ = 243 calls at the bottom for each request, just when it is failing
Each retry opens a new connection, and the service runs out of sockets long before it runs out of CPU
items.why: Retries at every layer multiply. Retry at one layer, cap the tries, and use a retry budget so a failing service sees less load, not more.

items.ask: Why add random jitter to exponential backoff?
choices: Clients that failed together otherwise back off by the same amounts and return together, in waves the server cannot serve
Random waits make it harder for an attacker to predict when a client will retry and to block its calls
Jitter shortens each client's waits on average, so a client gets through sooner than it would with plain exponential backoff
items.why: Backoff alone keeps the clients in step. A random wait up to the backoff spreads them over the interval, cutting both total calls and the time until all get through.

items.ask: What does a circuit breaker on calls to a slow dependency do?
choices: It retries each failed call immediately on a different replica of the dependency, until one of them answers
It slows down the caller's whole request rate until the dependency's error rate falls below a threshold
After repeated failures it fails calls at once, with a fallback, and later lets a few through as a test
items.why: Failing fast frees the caller's threads and takes load off the dependency so it can recover. The half-open test decides when to resume.

items.ask: An API server gives calls to its recommendations service their own pool of 40 threads, apart from its main pool of 200. What does that buy?
choices: Recommendations are answered 40 at a time in parallel, so they come back about forty times faster
If recommendations get slow, at most 40 threads wait on them and the other 160 keep serving everything else
Recommendations can never time out, because they always have threads of their own reserved for them
items.why: That is a bulkhead: a limit on how much of the caller one dependency can tie up. Calls beyond the 40 are refused at once and go to the fallback.

items.ask: A server is overloaded. Which response helps the system recover rather than spreading the trouble?
choices: Let the load balancer's health check remove the slow server, so that its share of traffic goes to the others
Queue every request until it can be served, so that no user's request is ever turned away
Refuse low-priority requests early and cheaply, before doing any work on them, and keep serving the rest
items.why: Load shedding keeps the server doing useful work. Removing it piles its load on its neighbours, which then fail too; queuing everything makes every request late.

items.ask: Why did Netflix run Chaos Monkey in production during working hours?
choices: A test environment lacks production's traffic and real dependencies, and in working hours the owners are at hand
Working hours had the most viewers, so a failure then showed its largest effect on stream starts and was easiest to measure against the noise
Machines killed at night came back more slowly, which would have hidden how fast recovery could be
items.why: Failure-handling code runs only when something fails, and only production has the real traffic and dependencies to fail against. Running failures on purpose finds weak spots on your schedule, with people ready, instead of at 3 a.m. Viewing peaks in the evening, not in working hours.

summary: **A slow dependency is worse than a dead one.** Threads in use are rate × time held, so a call that slows from 30 ms to 3 s can fill a whole pool and stop unrelated requests.
**Every call needs a timeout and a fallback.** Set the timeout just above the dependency's 99.9th percentile, and return something honest when it fires.
**Retries help with one-off faults and hurt with overload.** Retry at one layer only, cap the tries, and keep retries within a budget.
**Retries multiply down a chain.** Three tries at each of five layers can send 243 calls to the bottom for one request.
**Back off, with jitter.** Doubling waits spread retries over time; randomness stops clients that failed together from returning together.
**A circuit breaker fails fast.** After enough failures it skips the dependency for a while, then tests it, giving both sides room to recover.
**A bulkhead caps what one dependency can take.** A separate small pool of threads keeps a slow service from using up the rest.
**Shed load early and by priority.** Refusing cheaply is better than queuing work that will time out, and better than pulling slow servers out of rotation.
**Test failure on purpose.** Chaos Monkey and its successors made failure-handling code run every day, in production, with its owners at hand.

migration.title: Seven years to move
migration.text: Netflix's account of the move, published when it finished in January 2016, says the 2008 corruption was the reason, and that it chose to rebuild its services for the cloud rather than move the old ones over as they were.

aws.title: The April 2011 outage
aws.text: A network change in one availability zone left many of Amazon's Elastic Block Store volumes trying to copy themselves at once, and the storage system jammed. Netflix had kept its services from depending on those volumes and ran in several zones, so losing some of them hurt less.

default.title: Defaults that wait for ever
default.text: Java's standard HttpURLConnection, for instance, has connect and read timeouts of zero, which means no limit. A call to a server that accepts the connection and never answers holds its thread until the process is restarted.

budget.title: Retry budgets
budget.text: A budget counts retries against first tries over a recent window, and a client stops retrying when it is spent. Google's SRE book describes a limit of retries at 10% of requests per client, alongside at most three tries per request.

fuse.title: From the fuse box
fuse.text: An electrical circuit breaker trips when the current is too high, so a fault in one appliance does not set the house's wiring on fire, and it must be reset once the fault is fixed. The software version resets itself by testing, since nobody wants to be paged to flip it back.

sps.title: Stream starts per second
sps.text: Netflix chose this as its measure of health because it follows what members do: when something breaks, people press play and nothing happens, and the rate falls within seconds. Its weekly and daily rhythm is regular enough that a dip stands out.
